domains.title: Hwanung, the Heavenly Prince
domains.subtitle: descended bringer of law, grain, and civilisation
domains.lead: Hwanung is the heavenly prince who descends from the court of Hwanin to bring law, agriculture, and the arts of civilisation to earth in Korean tradition. The name means "Heavenly prince" and belongs to the domain "Son of Heaven, Descended." Hwanung is the son of Hwanin and the father of Dangun in the founding myth cycle recorded in the Samguk Yusa. He descends to earth beneath a sandalwood tree on a high mountain, bringing three heavenly seals and three thousand retainers.

cards.name: Son of Hwanin
cards.desc: Hwanung carries the authority of heaven as the delegate of his father, the Lord of Heaven.

cards.name: Descended to Taebaek
cards.desc: He descends beneath a sandalwood tree on a high mountain, the sacred entry point between heaven and earth.

cards.name: Law and Agriculture
cards.desc: He teaches the people law, grain, medicine, and the crafts that define civilised life.

cards.name: Father of Dangun
cards.desc: His union with Ungnyeo produces Dangun, the first ancestor and king of the Korean people.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Hwanung is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

myths.title: The Descent from Heaven
myths.text: Yearning to rule the world below, Hwanung asked his father Hwanin to send him to earth. Hwanin granted him three heavenly seals and three thousand retainers, and Hwanung descended to a sandalwood tree on the slopes of a high mountain.

myths.title: The Rule of Wind and Rain
myths.text: Hwanung governed the natural forces that sustain agriculture: wind, rain, clouds, and grain. Under his rule the people learned the arts of civilisation, including law, medicine, and the weaving of cloth.

myths.title: The Birth of Dangun
myths.text: When a bear and a tiger begged to become human, Hwanung tested them with garlic and mugwort. The bear endured and became a woman, Ungnyeo; she married Hwanung and gave birth to Dangun, founder of Gojoseon.

etymology.derivation: The name combines 桓 (hwan, "majestic, spreading") and 雄 (ung, "male, hero"). Read 환웅 in Korean, it denotes the heroic son of heaven whose descent initiates Korean civilisation.

originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Hwanung, the Hangul form is 환웅 and the Hanja form is 桓雄. Hangul ‘환웅’ and Hanja ‘桓雄’, the forms preserved in the Samguk Yusa. The ASCII form hwanung is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Hwanung is the scholarly citation form.
syncretism: Hwanung functions as a culture-hero in the Korean mythic system, comparable to other East Asian figures who descend from heaven to teach agriculture and law. The story has been read through Confucian, Buddhist, and Daoist lenses, each tradition finding in it a model of virtuous rule or cosmic harmony. In modern Korean nationalism, Hwanung represents the heavenly origin of Korean civilisation, while in shamanic ritual he is remembered as one of the high spirits of the celestial pantheon.
culturalLegacy: Hwanung appears in national foundation pageants, school textbooks, museum displays, and cultural diplomacy. The myth of his descent is dramatised at the annual Dangun memorial rites and in television dramas that retell the founding story. The figure also informs Korean environmental thought: the mountain of descent, often identified with Baekdu or Taebaek, remains a sacred landscape. In digital spaces, Hwanung is invoked by those who see Korean civilisation as uniquely endowed with a heaven-granted mandate.
extendedMeditation: Hwanung invites reflection on the relationship between name, place, and identity. The restoration of the capitalised scholarly form is a small act of recognition: it marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance in Korean culture and resists the flattening effect of ASCII-only domain names.
